<item xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/">
			<title>Thread-identity switcheroo for io_uring</title>
			<link>https://lwn.net/Articles/1094303/</link>
			<guid>https://lwn.net/Articles/1094303/</guid>
			<dc:creator>corbet</dc:creator>
			<description>The <a
href="https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/io_uring.7.html">io_uring
subsystem</a> is all about asynchronous execution; applications count on it
to not block — unless explicitly requested to.  Within io_uring, maintaining
the "never blocks" guarantee has sometimes been a challenge, given that
many paths in the kernel were never designed for asynchronous execution.
This problem has been worked around, but at a significant cost to
performance.  Now, io_uring maintainer Jens Axboe has posted <a
href="https://lwn.net/ml/all/20260911154148.644489-1-axboe@kernel.dk">an RFC patch set</a>
with a somewhat radical (and potentially scary) solution to the problem.
</description>
			<pubDate>Thu, 01 Oct 2026 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
		</item>

			<description>The <a href="https://git-scm.com/">Git</a> source-code management system is
at the core of development processes worldwide, so changes, especially
incompatible changes, are of great interest to the developers involved.
The Git 2.56 release, which can be expected around the end of September, is
currently available in <a
href="https://lwn.net/ml/all/xmqqh5jpvzxo.fsf@gitster.g">release-candidate</a> form.  It
is not the most earth-shaking of releases, but the one that follows, which
might be the long-awaited Git 3.0, may well be.
</description>
			<pubDate>Thu, 01 Oct 2026 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
		</item>

<item xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/">
			<title>Testing compat_linux on NetBSD with the Linux Test Project</title>
			<link>https://lwn.net/Articles/1094310/</link>
			<guid>https://lwn.net/Articles/1094310/</guid>
			<dc:creator>jzb</dc:creator>
			<description><p><a href="https://netbsd.org/">NetBSD</a> has long had support for
running Linux binaries via its kernel-level <a
href="https://man.netbsd.org/compat_linux.8"><tt>compat_linux</tt></a>
feature, but test coverage for it was less complete than some might
hope. In order to provide better testing for <tt>compat_linux</tt>,
Google Summer of Code (GSoC) participant Henrique Brito opted to work
on enabling the <a
href="https://linux-test-project.readthedocs.io/en/latest/">Linux Test
Project (LTP)</a> test suite to compile and run on NetBSD. At <a
href="https://2026.eurobsdcon.org/">EuroBSDCon&#160;2026</a>, Brito's
mentor, Stephen Borrill, provided a report on the project, and the
status of LTP on NetBSD. The work has already resulted in some minor
fixes, and a good list of additional problems to solve.</p>
</description>
			<pubDate>Thu, 01 Oct 2026 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
		</item>

<item xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/">
			<title>Compiling the kernel with gccrs</title>
			<link>https://lwn.net/Articles/1095553/</link>
			<guid>https://lwn.net/Articles/1095553/</guid>
			<dc:creator>daroc</dc:creator>
			<description><p>
Pierre-Emmanuel Patry and Arthur Cohen gave a talk at
<a href="https://rustconf.com/">
RustConf&#160;2026</a> on the
status of the Rust frontend for GCC (gccrs), with a particular eye toward the
goal of
<a href="https://lwn.net/Articles/1083202/">
compiling the Linux kernel</a>. Patry gave a follow-up talk for a more
kernel-focused audience at
<a href="https://kangrejos.com/">
Kangrejos</a> the next week, which Cohen could not attend. The
<a href="https://rust-gcc.github.io/">
gccrs project</a> is
making good progress overall, but it will still be some time until the compiler
is usable.
</p>
</description>
			<pubDate>Thu, 01 Oct 2026 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
		</item>

<item xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/">
			<title>Ideas on modernizing the open-source desktop</title>
			<link>https://lwn.net/Articles/1095425/</link>
			<guid>https://lwn.net/Articles/1095425/</guid>
			<dc:creator>jzb</dc:creator>
			<description><p>Scott Jenson has been working on user interfaces (UIs) and user experience (UX)
for many years at Apple, Google, and other companies. Now, he's trying to convince
open-source projects to experiment more and drive the desktop beyond the age-old "<a
href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WIMP_(computing)">windows, icons, menus,
pointer</a>" (WIMP) model. At <a
href="https://akademy.kde.org/2026/">Akademy&#160;2026</a>, KDE's annual developer
conference, he shared his complaints and ideas in a talk aimed
at convincing those in attendance to take the lead on desktop design.</p>
</description>

		</item>

<item xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/">
        <title>Listening to the radio with Rust</title>
        <link>https://lwn.net/Articles/1095721/</link>
        <guid>https://lwn.net/Articles/1095721/</guid>
        <dc:creator>daroc</dc:creator>
        <description><p>
Many of the transmissions sent over the radio spectrum can
be decoded with a relatively cheap hardware dongle. Thomas Eckert presented at
<a href="https://rustconf.com/">
RustConf 2026</a> in Montreal about his hobby:
decoding radio transmissions with Rust.
In his presentation, he
covered all of the math necessary to get started with
<a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Software-defined_radio">
software-defined radio</a>,
and gave demonstrations of listening to AM and FM radio, as well as decoding
transmissions from
aircraft transponders. His slides and example code are
<a href="https://github.com/t-eckert/listening-to-the-radio-with-rust#listening-to-the-radio-with-rust">
available</a> on GitHub.
</p>
</description>
        <pubDate>Thu, 08 Oct 2026 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
        </item>

<item xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/">
        <title>How KDE got funding to add enterprise features</title>
        <link>https://lwn.net/Articles/1096245/</link>
        <guid>https://lwn.net/Articles/1096245/</guid>
        <dc:creator>jzb</dc:creator>
        <description><p>The <a href="https://www.sovereign.tech/">Sovereign Tech Agency</a> (STA) is
<a href="https://www.sovereign.tech/tech/kde">investing nearly €1.3 million</a>
in KDE through 2027. At <a href="https://akademy.kde.org/2026/">Akademy 2026</a>
in Graz, Austria, Nate Graham and Kevin Ottens, two of the contributors who
helped bring in the investment, explained how the funding was secured, provided
tips on how projects should approach organizations like STA, and talked about
how that money will be improving KDE for everyone. In addition to keeping the
community informed about the work, the pair hoped to pass on what they have learned
to encourage others to help raise funds for development as well.</p>
</description>
        <pubDate>Thu, 08 Oct 2026 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
        </item>

<item xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/">
        <title>Reducing undefined behavior in the C language</title>
        <link>https://lwn.net/Articles/1095811/</link>
        <guid>https://lwn.net/Articles/1095811/</guid>
        <dc:creator>corbet</dc:creator>
        <description>As a professor of biomedical engineering, Martin Uecker perhaps does not
fit the profile of a typical presenter at <a
href="https://kernel-recipes.org/en/2026/">Kernel Recipes</a>.  He is,
however, a longtime Linux user, and works on free software for controlling
magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scanners.  He was at the conference to
talk about the C programming language, the specific problem of undefined
behavior in C, and whether it can eventually be made into a memory-safe
language.
</description>
        <pubDate>Thu, 08 Oct 2026 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
        </item>

<item xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/">
        <title>The kernel from a PostgreSQL point of view</title>
        <link>https://lwn.net/Articles/1096827/</link>
        <guid>https://lwn.net/Articles/1096827/</guid>
        <dc:creator>corbet</dc:creator>
        <description>Andres Freund has <a href="https://lwn.net/Articles/967866/">a few claims to fame</a>, but
chief among them is his many years of work to improve the performance of
the <a href="https://postgresql.org/">PostgreSQL</a> relational database
management system.  That work requires working with — or around — many
Linux kernel features and behaviors.  He put in an appearance at the 2026
edition of <a href="https://kernel-recipes.org/en/2026/">Kernel Recipes</a>
to talk about his experience working with the kernel project, how the
kernel could better support applications like PostgreSQL, and some
interesting developments in the PostgreSQL world.
</description>
        <pubDate>Thu, 08 Oct 2026 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
        </item>

<item xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/">
        <title>Native support for Rust on the GPU</title>
        <link>https://lwn.net/Articles/1095731/</link>
        <guid>https://lwn.net/Articles/1095731/</guid>
        <dc:creator>daroc</dc:creator>
        <description><p>
Christian Legnitto is the maintainer of
<a href="https://github.com/Rust-GPU/rust-gpu#-rust-gpu">
rust-gpu</a> and
<a href="https://github.com/Rust-GPU/rust-cuda#the-rust-cuda-project">
Rust CUDA</a>, two
libraries that make it possible to program a computer's graphics processing unit
(GPU) from Rust. He isn't satisfied with the current state of GPU support in
Rust, however. In a talk at
<a href="https://rustconf.com/">
RustConf 2026</a>, he explained his vision for how the
GPU could become an ordinary compiler target for normal Rust code, without the
need for any special libraries or new ecosystem support. That vision is not yet
fully implemented, but he does have a prototype that he is preparing to release.
</p>
</description>
        <pubDate>Thu, 08 Oct 2026 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
        </item>

<item xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/">
        <title>The year in Plasma and what's ahead</title>
        <link>https://lwn.net/Articles/1096518/</link>
        <guid>https://lwn.net/Articles/1096518/</guid>
        <dc:creator>jzb</dc:creator>
        <description><p>A lot has happened in the <a href="https://kde.org/plasma-desktop/">KDE
Plasma desktop environment</a> in the last year. Marco Martin, a KDE contributor
who spends most of his time working on Plasma, took the stage at <a
href="https://akademy.kde.org/2026/">Akademy 2026</a> in Graz, Austria to give
an update on Plasma's major new features, some of the minor-but-interesting
ones, and a preview of what's coming soon. The biggest upcoming change, dropping
X11 support from Plasma, has been well-advertised; but there are also plans
afoot to further improve remote-desktop support and more.</p>
</description>
        <pubDate>Thu, 08 Oct 2026 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
        </item>

<item xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/">
        <title>Comparing Chromium development at Google and Igalia</title>
        <link>https://lwn.net/Articles/1094721/</link>
        <guid>https://lwn.net/Articles/1094721/</guid>
        <dc:creator>jake</dc:creator>
        <description>Sharon Yang is a <a href="https://www.chromium.org/Home/">Chromium</a> developer who worked at Google on the browser
and now works on it at Igalia.  On the final day of FOSSY 2026, she gave a
presentation on her experiences with both of those companies, comparing and
contrasting the ways the each operates and how that affects work on the
code base.  She enjoyed working at Google and feels the same about Igalia,
so the talk was not aimed at complaints—instead it was meant to give a feel
for two companies that are rather different.
</description>

        </item>

<item xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/">
        <title>Coping with the onslaught of kernel security bugs</title>
        <link>https://lwn.net/Articles/1096908/</link>
        <guid>https://lwn.net/Articles/1096908/</guid>
        <dc:creator>corbet</dc:creator>
        <description>By now it is no secret that large language models (LLMs) have made it easy
for people to identify security bugs, and that has resulted in a flood of
bug reports to almost every free-software project, including the kernel.
At the 2026 edition of <a href="https://kernel-recipes.org/en/2026/">Kernel
Recipes</a>, Greg Kroah-Hartman took the stage to talk about how the
kernel's security team is handling this deluge.  His core message was
"<q>don't panic</q>".
</description>
        <pubDate>Thu, 15 Oct 2026 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
        </item>

<item xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/">
        <title>Beyond the &</title>
        <link>https://lwn.net/Articles/1096028/</link>
        <guid>https://lwn.net/Articles/1096028/</guid>
        <dc:creator>daroc</dc:creator>
        <description><p>
Rust has a number of kinds of smart pointers, both in the standard
library and defined by users. Still, some operations that are possible with
built-in references are not possible to perform with user-defined smart
pointers. Tyler Mandry, lead of the Rust project's
<a href="https://rust-lang.org/governance/teams/#team-lang">
language team</a>, spoke at
<a href="https://rustconf.com/">
RustConf 2026</a> about the lengthy effort to change that, and make smart pointers
just as flexible as built-in references.
</p>
</description>
        <pubDate>Thu, 15 Oct 2026 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
        </item>
